title: Dependent Arising — nothing stands alone
when: Associated with the Buddha’s teachings, usually placed around the fifth century BCE, though his dates are debated; the surviving discourses were transmitted orally and took shape over generations.
people: The Buddha (Gautama); later Buddhist interpreters across multiple traditions
origin: North India’s Gangetic region, within the wider community of wandering śramaṇa movements
idea: Dependent arising (Pāli paṭiccasamuppāda; Sanskrit pratītyasamutpāda) is the principle that phenomena occur in dependence on conditions: when relevant conditions arise, something else can arise; when they cease, its dependent result can cease. Early Buddhist texts apply this especially to the arising and ending of suffering. A familiar twelve-link formulation traces a process from ignorance through craving and grasping to birth, aging, and death, but it should not be mistaken for a simple, single-cause chain: conditions work amid multiple circumstances. The teaching also challenges the idea of a permanent, self-sufficient person or thing. It does not say that everything is connected to everything else, nor that nothing exists; it emphasizes specific conditional relations and the possibility of change when conditions change.
relevance: The idea offers a way to think about problems without reducing them to isolated causes or fixed essences. In personal life, institutions, and ecology, it directs attention to the conditions that sustain a pattern—and to which conditions might be altered. It also encourages intellectual modesty: what appears independent may rely on relationships we have overlooked.
